questions.question: Why does a page built entirely from <div> elements cause problems for screen reader users specifically?
options: Screen readers cannot render div elements at all
div elements create no landmarks, so a screen reader announces everything generically and the user must listen through content linearly instead of jumping to a region
div elements are slower to load than semantic elements
It only affects users on mobile devices
questions.explanation: Landmarks like <nav> and <main> let screen reader users jump directly to a page region, the audio equivalent of a sighted user's eye jumping straight to the navbar.

questions.question: What is the key distinguishing test for choosing <article> over <section>?
options: article is for anything with a heading, section is for anything without one
Whether the content would still make sense if distributed or syndicated completely on its own, independent of the page around it
There is no real difference, they are interchangeable
questions.explanation: article is for self-contained content (a blog post, a product card); section is for a thematic grouping that's part of a larger whole, not standalone.

questions.question: Why does skipping heading levels (e.g. <h1> directly to <h4>) cause a problem?
options: It's purely a visual/font-size issue with no other consequence
It breaks the document outline that both screen readers (heading navigation) and search engines rely on to understand content hierarchy
Browsers will refuse to render the page
It only matters for pages longer than one screen
questions.explanation: Heading levels form a nested outline; skipping levels (or using them purely for font size) breaks that structure for anyone or anything navigating by heading hierarchy.

questions.question: When is it appropriate to use a plain <div> instead of a semantic element?
options: Never — div should always be avoided entirely
When no semantic element (header, nav, main, article, section, footer, etc.) accurately describes the content's role, and the element exists purely for styling/layout
questions.explanation: div is semantically neutral — appropriate as a last resort for styling hooks, not as the default building block for every piece of structure.
